claims.text: Nearly equiatomic quinary high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are intrinsically thermally unstable at elevated temperatures.
Surface energy and chemical short-range order dominate configurational entropy in these nanoparticles.
Elevated-temperature evolution of the nanoparticles will produce spontaneous clustering and phase separation rather than preservation of a disordered solid solution.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles amplifies the thermodynamic driving force for elemental segregation.
For multicomponent alloys, the number of interacting pairs scales as N squared, whereas configurational entropy scales as N ln N.
The N-squared versus N ln N scaling makes chemical ordering especially dominant at the nanoscale.
CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm can initially exist as disordered solid solutions.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi can form an initially disordered solid-solution structure.
Chemical short-range order and surface-segregation driving forces promote local clustering followed by phase decomposition.
Configurational entropy can be insufficient to prevent chemically driven clustering in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
Negative mixing enthalpies of selected atomic pairs drive the proposed nanoparticle instability.
Surface-energy minimization drives elemental segregation in the proposed nanoparticles.
Atomic rearrangement can produce a clustering-to-ordering transition in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
Heating will rapidly form chemical clusters and separated phases, eliminate the initial disordered structure, and make the nanoparticles less thermally stable than bulk counterparts.
Traditional high-entropy-alloy concepts attribute elevated-temperature solid-solution stability to high configurational entropy.
Nanoparticles larger than approximately 50 nm should recover bulk-like behavior and fall outside the hypothesis.
Systems with near-zero mixing enthalpy and negligible short-range-order driving forces should fall outside the hypothesis.
Retention of a disordered solid solution without detectable clustering or phase separation after prolonged heating at 800 K would falsify the proposed intrinsic instability.

contradictions.description: Al0.1CrCoFeNi is presented as an example of a nearly equiatomic alloy composed of five transition metals, but Al is not a transition metal and the formula corresponds to only about 2.4 at.% Al, so it is not nearly equiatomic.
